opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. AI coding tools have made engineering dramatically faster. A single good engineer with the right tools can now build in days what used to take a small team weeks. So in many cases, yes, teams can and probably should be smaller, but the more interesting part is where the bottleneck moves.

When building software becomes cheap and fast, the constraint shifts to deciding *what* to build. Product management, talking to users, forming a clear point of view on what customers need: that becomes the slow step. I've seen teams where the ratio of engineers to product managers used to be something like six or eight to one, and some people are now proposing much lower ratios, even closer to one to one. Not because PMs suddenly got more important in the abstract, but because engineering got so much faster that product decisions became the limiting factor.

So my advice is usually not "cut headcount." It's "rethink the shape of the team." Small, tight teams where the people building also have strong product instincts tend to move incredibly fast. An engineer who can talk to a user, form a hypothesis, build a prototype that afternoon, and get feedback the next day is enormously valuable right now. Fewer handoffs, less coordination overhead, faster iteration loops.

There's also a nuance on risk. For quick prototypes, small teams can move fast and break things, because if a prototype fails nobody's hurt. For production systems touching real customers, you still need care around reliability, security, and responsible deployment. So smaller teams for exploration, with appropriate rigor once something is shown to work.

Net, I'm very optimistic. Small teams have more leverage today than at any point I can remember, and the ones that learn to use these tools well, and pair that speed with good judgment about what to build, will run circles around much larger organizations.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether teams should be smaller and how to reshape them, but does not raise whether organizations are overinvesting or underinvesting.

fable-5.1.text:
I think teams should be smaller today, and I actually think a lot of founders already sense this but haven't fully updated their playbook.

Here's the thing. For a long time, the way you scaled a software company was you hired more engineers. If you wanted to build more features, you added more people. Now, with AI coding tools, a single engineer can do much more than they could even two years ago. So the question becomes: do I need ten engineers, or do I need three really good engineers who are very fluent with these tools?

What I've seen in a lot of the startups I work with is that small teams of, say, four to six people are now able to build things that would have taken twenty or thirty people a few years ago. And a smaller team has real advantages beyond cost. Communication overhead goes down dramatically. Everyone can actually hold the whole product in their head. Decisions get made in a hallway conversation instead of a planning meeting.

There's also a hiring angle that I think is underappreciated. When I'm hiring now, I care a lot more about whether someone has actually integrated these tools into how they work. Not whether they can write code from scratch, but whether they know how to direct an AI assistant, check its work, and move fast. Someone who's really good at that is worth several people who aren't. So you don't need as many hires, but each hire matters more.

Now, I don't want to overstate it. There are still things that need headcount. If you're doing sales across many regions, if you're doing a lot of customer support, if you're building hardware, you still need people. And there's still a floor on team size for things like having someone on call, having redundancy, that sort of thing.

But my honest advice to founders is to resist the instinct to hire as a signal of progress. Stay small longer than feels comfortable. Hire when you've exhausted what the current team plus AI tools can do, not before. I think the companies that figure this out will be more capital efficient, faster to iterate, and frankly more fun to work at.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether companies need as many engineers and advises delaying hires, which raises the possibility of overinvesting in headcount. It does not raise whether organizations might be underinvesting when choosing smaller teams.

astra-6.text:
I think teams can be smaller today, particularly when you’re trying to figure out what to build. With AI coding tools, a couple of engineers can test an idea much faster than they could before. So you can get something in front of users, learn what’s wrong with it, and iterate without first assembling a large team.

But I would distinguish between needing fewer people to do a fixed amount of work and wanting to do more work. If building software gets cheaper, there are a lot of applications that suddenly become worth building. So I don’t think the conclusion is simply that every company should have fewer engineers.

The question I’d ask is: Where is the bottleneck? If you can write code much faster, but you’re still taking weeks to decide what users need, adding more engineers probably won’t help. A small team with a clear problem, close contact with users, and the ability to make decisions quickly can be very effective.

r001.rationale: The response discusses smaller teams, engineering capacity, and whether more engineers help, but it does not raise whether organizations are overinvesting or underinvesting.

sol-6.1.text:
I think teams can be much smaller today, especially when you're exploring a new idea. With AI coding tools, one or two engineers can build something that would have taken a much larger team before. And that changes how you want to organize the work.

If you're still figuring out what users want, a small team can go through that loop much faster: build something, put it in front of users, learn, and change direction. Adding people also adds communication overhead, so I wouldn't assume that a larger team will get you to the answer faster.

But I don't think the conclusion is that every team should shrink. If the cost of building software falls, there are a lot more things worth building. So I'd think about giving small teams more ambitious goals, and running more experiments, rather than just doing the same work with fewer people.

r001.rationale: The response discusses smaller teams, lower software-building costs, and running more experiments, but it does not raise whether organizations are overinvesting or underinvesting.
